utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've asked for the witness to be kept out just for two minutes. First, just to deal with a tiny matter of administration about an exhibit that was dealt with yesterday, 2360.18. It was, I think, thought that the full version of that document was in the international armed conflict binder on investigation. It may not have been, or was not, in full in that binder, but may yesterday's supplied version now be the version that counts, with all the pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And just to register the Defence's objection, Your Honour, we contest the authenticity of that document. It looks like the two charts that I adverted to yesterday actually have numbers up on the top right-hand corner of them. They appear to be identification numbers from the Prosecution. Those identification numbers do not actually appear on the first two pages of the document. So without an adequate foundation being laid for the authenticity of that document, we contest it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the second point is a general point. I think I ought to register that the flow of information that we are receiving for these witnesses, generally -- I make no complaint about it. I'm just recording the fact -- means that we certainly can't prepare fully for witnesses as they come. It's beyond our resources to do so. We can only do the best that's available in the limited time. We will attempt not to apply for adjournments for cross-examination, but the position is as I described it. So far as the next witness is concerned, the position is particularly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us an example of that, Mr. Nice, to show how -- in relation to the flow of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. When the witness statement comes, or summary comes, it may provide, for the first time, detailed information that is new that we have to deal with. In any event, we've only had a few days or weeks to know that a large number of witnesses are coming, and we're not in a position to research all that we might be able properly to research about those witnesses. Accordingly, when the witness comes to the witness seat, we're not in a position either to challenge or, alternatively, to accept, all that he says which may be new, nor are we necessarily in a position to help you by asking him all the questions that we would be if we had more time to research matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Generally how far ahead are you getting these statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We get the summaries basically the day before, sometimes a couple days before. And even getting them a couple days before doesn't mean that we're going to be in a position to do what we should for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's the case of the shoe being on other foot, because the Defence made pretty much the same kind of complaint during the presentation of the Prosecution case, and I think we have to make the best of it and have to ask for the cooperation of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's not a question of not cooperation, and I think Your Honour is wrong about saying that it's the same as the shoe on the other foot. Defence always know what both their cases are because they, from the beginning, have our case in full; they've had it for years in statements, and they know what their case is. We don't. It comes to us fresh. I'm not complaining. I'm quite prepared to do our best. But what I don't want you to think is that you're going to get the perfect performance that you'd have if, for example, we'd had, as you would in some civil cases, advance sight of witness statements and all the time in the world and the resources to prepare them. We can't do that. Now, that is a limitation on us, and it has one dangerous consequence. It has two dangerous consequences. One is that there may be things that witnesses are going to say that we should simply admit, because if we could research them, we could say, "Fine. That's not in issue," and that could then become an accepted fact. The second problem is the obvious one -- I make no complaint about it. I'm simply making an observation -- that we can't help you, sometimes, with the detailed cross-examination that might be possible if we had more time. With the witnesses coming today, for example, we had no knowledge that he was coming this week. We thought he was coming next week. A fax was apparently sent on the 28th. We've not been able to track it down. I don't say it wasn't sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I've got a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we haven't managed to find it. So the first I knew about this witness coming was yesterday morning. His summary had been sent the night before, at 6.00. It didn't reach me until yesterday morning, and it wouldn't have made any difference if it had met me the night before, because I was busy with the previous witness. So we will do the best we can in the time available, but subject to the limitations I've explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me, while we're on this topic, cover the more general matter which I raised with you the day before, which is the time available for this case. We now have three other cases to try. This case has occupied a year already. No doubt it inevitably is going to take some time. But there is pressure upon the Trial Chamber, and inevitably on everybody involved in the case, to finish it in order that other trials can take place. There may eventually be more resources available, but there may not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that is the real difficulty which we face. And so we have to balance fairness to all sides, of course, but also the need for expedition. I'll be grateful, as I'm sure you do, that you have that in mind, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We absolutely have that in mind, and our problem includes this: that if, for example, we see a witness and we think, "Fine. Well, we'll simply take just a couple of points with that witness and sit down and leave the rest for argument," then there's always the problem that the Chamber will be working on exiguous material and too limited material, one way or the other. We have no -- and for example, we had a problem, I think, with the witness two days ago. He raised new issues about Zenica and about Busovaca -- new entirely; they hadn't been raised in cross-examination of other witnesses -- about the nature of attacks on those places. Now, it would be the easiest thing in the world for me simply to pursue a policy of trying to find a couple of grounds to attack the credibility of the witness, and then, because he was a Defence witness, and say, "And by the way, what you're saying about this and that is wrong," without researching the matter, and leaving it like that. That wouldn't be very responsible. I've got to be careful. But we quite understand the difficulties of the Chamber and we will do everything we can to abbreviate cross-examination, making our own judgement of when it's safe to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, just a couple of minutes on several issues also very important before the witness comes in. Just a comment on what my learned colleague for the Prosecution just said. I have a letter which we sent on the 19th of April regarding the witness which is going to give evidence today, Marko Prskalo, the first one. So from this letter, it's clear that he was going to be called in this period. As far as the summaries are concerned, we turn them over to the Prosecution the moment it has been signed by the witness. It's the earliest moment that we can turn it over. Of course, the Prosecution has heard our opening statements. They know the general direction in which we're going. They know what the line of defence is, so to speak, and they can prepare for the cross-examination at any time. So that is the only comment that I have to make on that. But my real request has to do with the administrative issue. One of the planned witnesses -- two of the planned witnesses, Marinko Palavra, Ivica Kristo, have told us they cannot come. Ivica Kristo could not get out of his business obligations, and Marinko Palavra has some personal problems. He's asked for a delay, and now we're not sure when and if he's going to be able to come. Yesterday, we also told the Prosecutor of two problem witnesses. I will not give their names because one of them is asking for protective measures. They are not able to come this week, but rather they are coming next week. So these are sudden changes which were just sprung on us yesterday. We will furnish the new and revised list as soon as we are able, and we hope that we will not have any gaps in providing witnesses. The next issue I wanted to bring up was that one of the witnesses who is on our list for next week, that is, in the following days, a witness who is on our witness list called up our office and sent a document which he received from Carla Del Ponte in Busovaca, in which he's asked to report to the office of the Tribunal on the 4th, 5th, and 6th regarding a crime which took place in Kacuni in January 1993. This is a witness with whom we had spoken previously and he had agreed to come, but this letter from the Prosecutor has frankly scared him. Pursuant to Article 18(2) and Rule 39(1), the Prosecutor is free to conduct their investigations in a manner that they see fit, but after we had made our list of witnesses public, we believe that it would have been correct that the Prosecutor should first contact us and tell us that they want to talk to our witnesses. It is not only the witness Grubesic at issue here. He is only one of the four witnesses whose names we have submitted to the Tribunal on the 30th of March of this year. Our witnesses are beginning to feel this as pressure on them, and I am asking the Trial Chamber for advice, how to proceed in this matter. We had an obligation to notify the Prosecution on witnesses with whom we potentially wanted to speak, and we did so. I believe that it would be a minimum standard of equality of arms that we be provided the same courtesy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you raised this matter with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I received this last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think the sensible thing, first of all, is to have a word with the Prosecution and see what the position is. If it cannot be resolved, then clearly the simplest course is to raise it with the Trial Chamber. But the first step is to raise it with the Prosecution and see what the position is. See if they can assist in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. But I just wanted the Trial Chamber to be informed of this. Now, with the Trial Chamber's permission, we would like to call our next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'll call the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for the witness, Your Honours, I omitted to say one thing. Today we submitted a motion which is fairly urgent, and we would just like to bring your attention to it. I believe it will be delivered to you during the break this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prskalo.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is a retired Major, Marko Prskalo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, I just said your name. Mr. Prskalo, you were born on 19 September 1941 in the village of Voljice?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your village is located in the municipality of Uskoplje, previously known as Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are a Bosnian Croat by ethnicity, a Roman Catholic by religion, and a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live before the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Before the civil war of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I lived in Bugojno. This is a town in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, let me just advise you. You and I speak the same language, but we need to wait for your answers and my questions to be interpreted into the official languages. So please take a moment before you give your answers. Please tell me, where do you live now? You don't live in Bugojno; isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I live in the Republic of Croatia with my family at the moment in the town of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you not live in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Because after the war, I could not go back to my home in Bugojno after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Someone else is living in your house now?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, Muslims live in my house right now, that is, a Muslim family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are married and you have three children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, until mid-1997 you were in the HVO, and then you retired with the rank of Major?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are an economist by profession?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have had a political career. For a number of years, you were a member of the parliament first of Bosnia-Herzegovina and, after the Dayton Accords, of the parliament of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. I have been involved in politics for a long period of time, just as you said. After the conditions were met for the multi-party system in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the break-up of the Soviet Union, the democratic system was introduced in the former Yugoslavia, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. But as we know, the democratic system has still not spread throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia. In 1990, during the first democratic elections, I was elected to the House of Representatives, that is, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And also before these elections, I became involved and I joined the largest Croatian political party, the Croatian Democratic Union, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was elected the president of the HDZ for Bugojno, and in this position I stayed for about one year; that is, to the middle of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's take this step by step. When you said that you were the president of the Bugojno HDZ, Mr. Vladimir Soljic was also holding high positions in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the HZ HB was established on the 18th November 1991, and we showed you a document which is Z27, which is a copy of the decision on the establishment of HZ HB, you saw who had signed this decision on behalf of Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I saw this document, and I observed that on this -- that there was the signature of Mr. Vladimir Soljic there who had signed this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know this gentleman well because you studied together in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. We were both -- studied economy, economics, in Zagreb at the time. We were close even during those college days, and I recognise his signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're moving right along. We're at paragraph 11 of the summary. We know that Mr. Mate Boban was the president of the Presidency of the HZ HB. You know this directly, and you know that he was both the president and the supreme commander of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I know this. He was both the supreme commander and the president of the HZ HB, and later on the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, HR HB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mate Boban was president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna until a meeting which was held in Livno in February 1994, which you also attended as a member of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. I was invited to this meeting in Livno as a member of the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I witnessed Mr. Boban's resignation to his post.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. We are going to move to the topic which we name "Military Service". It's paragraph 12 and on. Following a referendum which was held on 29 February and 1 March 1992, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence on 6 March 1992. Mr. Prskalo, you took part in this referendum, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I took part in this referendum. And with your permission, I will make a brief comment on these events because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I explain the rules here. Witnesses are here, of course, to give evidence, and there are some matters which are relevant to the trial and there are some which are not, and it's for the Court to decide which are and which aren't. So would you concentrate, please, on just answering counsel's questions. Counsel will know what's relevant and what isn't, and of course we ultimately will be the arbiters of what is and what isn't relevant. So I do not mean to be discourteous, of course, in stopping you, but we'll get on more quickly if you would just concentrate, please, on answering the questions. Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just to keep it very brief and not to waste any time, it is a fact which has not been disputed that the Serbian Democratic Party boycotted the elections and a number of citizens did not go to vote. But the referendum succeeded because the Croats and the Muslims did come out and vote?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, despite the fact that the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared, this country could not continue, because when the Bosnian Serb army attacked Mostar, it became clear to you that the war, which had raged and was waning in Croatia, would also hit Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. This was clear to us even earlier when the Croatian village of Ravno was attacked in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And immediately after the aggression of the Bosnian Serb army, Sarajevo was occupied and sealed, and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina reached a decision, declaring the imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that was on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And immediately after that, Mr. Mate Boban signed a decision establishing the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: That is correct too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a provisional necessity, because you needed to organise your Defence, since you already knew what had happened before.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Had it not been for that organisation, I believe that the Croats, the Croat people in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole, would have fared much worse than it actually did, and we did fare rather bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if my previous question was not precise enough. I said nothing. But the decision to set up the Croat Defence Council was adopted on the 8th of April, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, you joined the HVO in June 1991, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. I joined the HVO in June 1992, and it was at the time when the seat of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia was in Uskoplje, which is better known by its earlier name, Gornji Vakuf. Towards the end of June of that same year, Colonel Blaskic was appointed the commander, and I was then tasked to head the office for public relations and promotional activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us make it clear. You came to the practice between Ivan Zubo [phoen], who was leaving, and the period of time when Colonel Blaskic took the office, and you arrived there between those two events. Paragraph 17 of the summary. Will you please be so kind and tell us: You told us that you were tasked with the office of promotion and public relation, but people in the HVO were not allowed to engage in politics, so were you politically active, I mean in the political parties, or did you do something else?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: We who were in the HVO did not engage in politics in this sense, because political work was prohibited in the Croat Defence Council. Our duty went in a completely different direction and related mostly to information, then boosting the morale of the soldiers, taking care of the mental health of HVO soldiers. We were not in a situation to engage in politics, because political parties were engaged in politics and they were outside the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You listed some of the activities. You said education of soldiers made part of your duty.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was also one of the tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, tell us: In the Operative Zone -- and I'm talking about what you might be familiar with -- you held special press conferences. I believe it was in Bila. And there you informed both the citizens in your region and the International Community about the events about specific developments related to the troops of the Croat Defence Council, and these press conferences were attended by foreign newspapermen, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. We held press conferences. And there were also special press conferences which were held by politicians, or rather political officials. And the press conferences held by army representatives were a different thing. That is, they were held by the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. I can also say that our press conferences were -- used to be attended by politicians, that is, political figures. And I remember, for instance, that in addition to Colonel Blaskic, who attended those press conferences, and he mostly addressed military issues and developments in Central Bosnia, but -- and not always, but Mr. Dario Kordic would come now and then, and he would usually address political developments or he would, for instance, speak about the requests of the International Community or introduce some political conclusions. And others also attended those conferences from time to time, such as, for instance, Mr. Valenta, who would, as a rule, address economic topics, that is, economic subjects and developments in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us clarify this. There were press conferences which had to do exclusively with the army, and press conferences where political officials and the commander of the Operative Zone -- that is, as a rule, Colonel Blaskic, were another matter; there were different kinds of press conferences?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also sometimes attended those other press conferences in addition to Colonel Blaskic. I mean, those which were attended not only by politicians but also by government representatives, Mr. Valenta, for instance, whom you mentioned, and who was a member of the government. So you would also be there if it was necessary to read a proclamation or something, or what?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. I was present at those conferences from time to time, and it was my task to read a proclamation related to some event or a statement, communication, a press release, having to do with military developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us move on to chapter D, paragraphs 19 and 20. Mr. Prskalo, you are aware that the Prosecution is trying to prove in this case that you, the Bosnian Croats, are responsible for a systematic, planned, methodical policy of persecution, not only of Muslims, but all other people who are not of Croat ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I wish to say that that is not true, because that is not so in real life. Namely, we need to know all the things that were going on in the lands of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In particular, I wish to point out that in 1992, when the Serbs launched large-scale and brutal offensives throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, precisely by attacking Croat villages and towns, and also Muslim villages and towns, under those circumstances, the Serbs, who had their own policy and their -- and wanted to keep the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina within Yugoslavia, because their policy was -- that is, the policy of the Serb Democratic Party -- was that they, as a people, should all remain in one state, which is simply insane and beyond comprehension, because it was not possible in any sovereign country in this world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shouldn't really cut in, because we shall be losing the interpretation, but can't we move step by step, please.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just given us the background. You have just told us against which backdrop these things were happening in Bosnia in late 1992. And if we look at the end of 1992 and then 1993, Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you were located in different places, you were, to all intents and purposes, surrounded in some enclaves?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Bosnian Croats, especially in Central Bosnia, were in small enclaves, compressed in small areas in very narrow space. And I think it is beyond comprehension to accept that the Bosnian Croats tried to expel anyone, regardless of what people one is talking about, because our number was much lower. And, for instance, in Central Bosnia we had an enclave which was in Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, then the enclave in Vares, then an enclave in Kiseljak, and so on and so forth. There were more of them. But if we remember that those enclaves were surrounded in part by Serbs and in part by Croats, then it's simply impossible to understand how the Croats could try or planned to persecute anyone; namely, because such policy did not exist either amongst our politicians, nor did anyone ever advocate such policy of persecution of other peoples. Namely, our principle objective was to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in my activities, I addressed this topic on various occasions. There are documents which lay particular emphasis on this fact that this was our primary objective.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You made a slip of the tongue. You said that the enclave was surrounded in part by Serbs and in part by Croats. You evidently meant Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, it must have been my slip of the tongue. It wasn't so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we're referring to these enclaves, may I just remind Your Honours that in table H in our Pre-Trial brief, we showed, we identified, the enclaves that are mentioned by the witness. So let us finish this topic. Have you ever heard any of your soldiers, commanders, your superiors, your subordinates, or anyone else, mention these inadvertent comments of policy of persecution of Muslims, or some other people?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I have never heard any one of our commanders, or soldiers, or even politicians, promote such policy; therefore, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that in this case an effort is made to prove that the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina had some command interrelationship with the commander of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, that they had something like political commissars as existed in the Soviet Union. But I think you are a very convenient person to tell us, because you were assistant commander for the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia for this information and educational work. So is this thesis correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I must say that this thesis is not correct. Let me say how I was appointed, and I also know very well how other assistants for promotional and educational activities were appointed. Namely, we were not zampolits. We were not assistants responsible for political -- assistant political commissars who had very broad powers as in the Soviet Union. Our duties were purely military, so that we were not in such a situation and in such a position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So apart from you, who were responsible for this, there was -- there did not exist a representative of the HDZ, or some other political representative, in the HVO at any level?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Not only was there not anyone from the HDZ, but we did not receive from that -- and that was the leading political party in Bosnia-Herzegovina among the Croats -- we never received any -- they never tried to intercede or to intervene in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Prskalo, you are talking about regular chain of command in the Operative Zone. The commander was Colonel Blaskic; in the adjacent zone, Colonel Siljak; and they were subordinated to their commander, that is, the Main Staff of HVO. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. They unquestionably accounted to the Main Staff of the HVO, and that is the regular chain of command, insofar as it was possible to maintain it, to sustain it, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And perhaps my final question about this. Throughout the time you spent at the command of the Operative Zone, did you ever hear, from other sources, or from Colonel Blaskic, or a third person, that a politician, member of a political party, ever tried to impose an order on Colonel Blaskic or issue instructions to him regarding combat operations or things like that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: While I worked there, I never heard that Colonel Blaskic was ever given an order by a politician. Not only that; I have never heard that care in areas, in regions where the HVO was active, that any commander of the HVO ever received any order or instruction from a politician. That did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Naumovski. I should like to ask Major Prskalo. Major, do you think that Colonel Blaskic acted completely autonomously, that he had full authority, you, who were a political man there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Well, he had such powers which had to do with his area of operation, as the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, and clearly his immediate superior was the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Bennouna, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where did Colonel Blaskic receive his instructions, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that he received his instructions from the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, moving on to Chapter E, fighting in Novi Travnik in October '92, paragraphs 21 to 23, a few questions only. You know that in October '92, BH army forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina stopped a convoy with HVO troops going to reinforce -- to assist the defenders of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I know that in October '92, that convoy was stopped. The HVO was sending troops to that front in Jajce, because at that time -- precisely at that time, that front was in peril. There was a danger that the Bosnian Serbs might take that area and make a breakthrough towards Travnik. So that column was stopped. If I might continue explaining what happened then. Simultaneously with that event, with that incident when the column was stopped, the BH army, Novi Travnik, attacked Bosnian Croats, that is, the positions of the HVO, with a view to taking an important area, and that is the military factory in Novi Travnik which was of strategic relevance, of fundamental importance for military operations. And under those circumstances, under those critical circumstances when Jajce had to be defended, the BH army made such incomprehensible moves. I must say here that those events and the beginning of war in Novi Travnik cost us a great deal. We lost Jajce, and that was a great damage, a great pity for both the Muslims and Croats, because we were allies and we were supposed to fight together against the aggressor, and at that time that was the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have given us the reason why the BH army attacked the HVO in Novi Travnik, and that is the Bratstvo factory. Tell us, did you, the Croats, ever manage to regain control of the factory after October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: After the Bratstvo factory was taken in October 1992, the Croats never succeeded in regaining the control over the Bratstvo factory in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you are familiar with a detail which has to do with who attacked whom in Novi Travnik. You know an HVO commander whose family remained on Kalinska Street?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I know that particular case. My colleagues told me that the best proof was that the family of an HVO commander stayed in Kalinska Street, and were it true, what the Muslim side was saying, that the Croats had attacked Muslims there, then the HVO commander wouldn't have been all that stupid to leave his family in Kalinska Street, which came under the Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. We can move on. Mr. Prskalo, you were designated a member of a joint commission which was formed by the HVO and ABiH after the fighting in Novi Travnik, and the purpose of the Joint Commission was to endeavour to achieve peace, to resolve problems, exchange prisoners, return material goods and the like; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I was a member of this commission, and there were two more members on our side; that is, as HVO representatives, Stanislav Nusbaum and Mr. Zvonko Vukovic. And we also had our counterparts from the ABiH side. We wanted to calm the situation down and then exchange the prisoners and, as you said, to recover some of the material resources. And by this, we primarily meant vehicles, because even some of the private vehicles had been seized and the like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question. Who designated you to that Joint Commission by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: We received the order from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the final question related to this: Was Mr. Kordic a member of the Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No. Mr. Kordic practically had nothing to do with it; nor was there any need for him to have any dealings with the commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did anyone mention him or --

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No. He was never mentioned; nor was there any reason to mention Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move on to Chapter F, fighting in Busovaca in January '93, paragraph 24 onward. My first question would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I would like to introduce a document. It will be easier to treat this matter in this way. This is a report which was written by Mr. Prskalo, as assistant commander of the Operative Zone, Central Bosnia, for information and public relations. It is a document of the 23rd of January, '93. Could the usher please give a copy to Mr. Prskalo, the version in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D206/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, the 23rd of January, '93, you being the assistant commander of the Operative Zone, Central Bosnia, for propaganda and information, you sent this to the Main Staff, that is, to the assistant commander there who was responsible for information and public relations. I should like to draw your attention to the third paragraph. Namely, what preceded the fighting in Busovaca in January '93 was numerous incidents. You mentioned one of these incidents in paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is correct. This is indeed a document which I wrote and signed, and here in the third paragraph it says, if I may -- do you want me to read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. There is no need for you to, because the Chamber has the copies. I'm interested only in this attack that you are describing on the secretary-general of the HDZ, Mr. Ignac Kostroman, who was saved by pure chance, as you put it. It was an attempt to abduct him on the 21st -- on the 23rd of January, 1993, in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, that did happen, and owing to fortunate circumstances, Mr. Ignac Kostroman was rescued because UNPROFOR was passing by at that moment. Had it not been for that vehicle, I am positive that Mr. Ignac Kostroman would not be alive today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just the date in the transcript, I said that the document was of the 23rd of January, and I asked you if you were referring to the incident which happened on the 20th or the 21st of January. And your answer was that you meant this incident, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I don't really know the date exactly, but it happened before -- a day or two before this moment, that is, before I wrote the report. It was a day or two before I wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is interesting also because of what paragraph 4 says and onward, where you speak about the Sarajevo Television, or Zenica, which were held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Prskalo, did you, on behalf of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, send any information or press releases to Sarajevo and Radio Zenica, which were held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I sent such information on various occasions. Unfortunately, I have to say that these releases were never released for the public, yet they were worded in a manner and with a view to establishing peace, because the Croats and the HVO, of course, did not want a war with Muslims; nor was it in their interest. They did not want a war with the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you wanted to use facts to refute the disinformation which was spread around?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not hear you. Were any of those releases published?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I believe I said in my presentation that never -- not any one , press release or my communication, was presented to the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us then move on, and that is the end of January 1993, the 25th of January, 1993, onward. You know that this was the real beginning of war, to set aside the previous incidents, but the real beginning of war between the HVO and the ABiH. Who attacked whom on the 25th of January, 1993, in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: When we talk about the war in Busovaca, I must say that the attack was carried out by the ABiH, and unfortunately this was obviously part of their strategy, their objective, to cut off the communication lines between Busovaca and Kiseljak. This attack was carried out from three sides. From one side, it was from the direction of Busovaca towards Kiseljak, and Croatian villages which are alongside Busovaca-Kiseljak road were attacked, Donje Polje, Gusti Grab, Oseliste, and the objective of the Muslim forces at that time was, in practical terms, to take control of the supply road. It was a very important strategic area for the ABiH to take. And the other two directions of attacks went from Zenica, and their objective was to block the road and to take the strategically-important villages of Merdani and Grablje. These are the villages which are located in such a way that the forces who held them practically controlled the road from Kaonik, that is, the intersection on the road between Busovaca and Vitez, and there's a turn-off for a T-junction to go to Zenica. The objective of their attack was the Dusina-Lasva villages. When the Muslim forces took this area, they achieved control over another very important supply route. I must say that during these operations, incomprehensible crimes took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're asked questions, then you can answer them, but you've answered the question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, I was not -- I did not interrupt you because I let you say things the way you saw them. But I'm just going to ask you one detail which we will come back to later. As a member of the Joint Busovaca Commission, as it was popularly known, you toured these villages in February and March after the attack, that is, Gusti Grab, Oseliste, Nezirovici, Donje Polje, Kacuni, Cep, and so on, and you had an opportunity to see the state that the Croatian houses were in. What did they look like when you visited there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Together with the Monitoring Mission, that was the Joint Commission, in fact, which included the European Monitors and then representatives of the HVO and representatives of the ABiH, we all toured these areas, and specifically the villages that you mentioned from Kacuni towards Bilalovac, and unfortunately it was terrible to see the state that those houses were in. They were very well built, but for the most part now, they had been destroyed, they were burned, and it was an ugly sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move on. Your Honours, another document. This is another report compiled by Mr. Prskalo on the 26th of January, 1993. While the document is being distributed, I would just like to say that the Trial Chamber will have an opportunity to see this, but this document refers to the events in Busovaca which took place on that very same day, the 26th of January, 1993. The English copy may be placed on the ELMO. It's a very short document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, this was your report?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, this is the report which I drafted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. I cannot see in the transcript -- when you mentioned the Croatian house, the transcript does not reflect that they were Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I did mention that they were Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Prskalo, in paragraph 1, you say that Zvonko Rajic, a platoon commander from Lasva, went there with three soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, the Muslim forces killed Mr. Zvonko Rajic and another 11 members of -- another 11 Croats in the Lasva. This was an abhorrent crime which took place there, and it is incomprehensible that such things could have happened. This was one of the first and most serious crimes that took place in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, when we spoke, you told us that one of the cameramen who were at that time in Dusina, in Zenica, showed you a videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to introduce this videotape. I would like to play just a short excerpt from it, a minute or two. It's a part of a much longer videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, let us have a number for the documentary exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D207/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us next have a number for the video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape will be marked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is an excerpt, is it, Mr. Naumovski?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A very short one, one or two minutes, and the videotape is much longer. We will provide a copy of the entire tape to the Prosecution. Can we have the videotape, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can freeze the frame here, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, you saw this videotape as early as 1993. Whose body is this? You see that a part of the body is missing, some organs have been removed.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: This is the body of Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can play it on. I think that there is very little left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this is enough. I think that this may be sufficient for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later on, you went to Dusina. You had information on who committed these crimes in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. I came to Dusina following these events with the Monitoring Mission. We also went to Lasva village. And according to the information which we had, these apparent crimes were committed by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. I also heard that members of the 305th Jajce Brigade also participated in this crime, and the members of the 17th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You also know that a number of civilians were taken to a camp?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. I had information that some 30 Croatian civilians were taken to the camp in Kacuni, a village under Muslim control, following these apparent crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the so-called Silo in Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, the Silo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in Dusina, did you have an opportunity to see the Croatian houses?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Croatian houses were devastated. We had a meeting with a small group of civilians who were frightened, and not knowing who we were, they were reluctant even to talk to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, during this fighting in Busovaca municipality, in the wider territory of Busovaca municipality, did you hear whether the Bosnian army shelled the town of Busovaca and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. The Bosnian Muslim army did attack the town of Busovaca and its surroundings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last question on this topic,

utterances.speaker: MR. PRSKALO
utterances.text: Did the HVO ever manage to regain control over these key communication lines that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: After these operations in Busovaca, after this war in Busovaca, the Croats never managed to regain control over these areas until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can move along. Just a couple of questions on the Busovaca Joint Commission. The Trial Chamber had an opportunity to hear quite a bit about it from other witnesses, but you were a member of it from the end of January, say, 30 January 1993, until the 10th of March, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were appointed to it by whose decision?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I was appointed to this joint commission by a decision of Colonel Blaskic. In addition to me, Mr. Franjo Nakic was also appointed to it. He was Chief of Staff of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a while you worked there together with him in this Joint Commission?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, we worked together in the Joint Commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question: Was Mr. Kordic ever invited to any of the meetings of this Joint Commission, or did he participate in any negotiations or any work in it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Mr. Kordic was never invited to such meetings, nor was he involved in any negotiations relating to its work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Moving on to paragraph 30. Several questions relating to the fighting in Vitez, or the continuation of war in April of 1993. It is not in dispute that on 16 April serious fighting broke out in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, this is indisputable. And I can confirm it, because I was there. But I must say that the 16th of April is not the actual beginning of war in Vitez, because one can say that the fighting started in the night of the 15th, when the Muslim forces attacked a plateau in the direction of Zenica, and that was the actual beginning of the war. We had fierce fighting there. And only the next day, on the 16th April, the fighting spread and intensified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about a very important feature. This was the feature Kuber, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, this is the feature Kuber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this feature is above the village of Loncari?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Loncari, Putis, and Jelena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the HVO lost first that high ground; they had to retreat downhill?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO soldiers had to withdraw, because that night the ABiH attack was very fierce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, given the duty that you had, you must have been informed of all the events in those days. Before this outbreak, there were a number of acts of provocation. There were abductions of officers and such?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. Before this intense conflict which started on the 16th, there was a series of provocations, especially in the days preceding this attack. And I would like to point out for this Trial Chamber an event which took place in the area of Novi Travnik, where, on the 13th of April, members of ABiH, and specifically 7th Muslim Brigade, carried out an abduction of three HVO officers and their driver. And after that there was another incident which to me again is incomprehensible. That was on the 15th April, in the early morning hours, when the commander of the HVO Brigade, Zivko Totic, was suddenly attacked. He was in a vehicle with his military escort, and people were riddled with bullets, and on that occasion -- may I continue? -- on that occasion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just deal with what's relevant. One point is, Mr. Prskalo, we've heard already a great deal of evidence, as you'll appreciate, in this case. So many of these incidents are not new to the Trial Chamber. We're familiar with them. And it would be best if you'd just concentrate on the parts which counsel wants to ask you about specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, Mr. Totic will come here and he will be able to give the full account. But this was an introduction to another question that I wanted to ask. You personally were present at an extraordinary press conference which took place on the day when commander Zivko Totic was abducted, and it was because of this abduction that the press conference was held?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I was a participant of this press conference. It was an extraordinary press conference which was called because of the abduction of Commander Totic. And in this press conference, I read a statement which related to this unhappy incident. And also Colonel Blaskic spoke during the conference, and Mr. Kordic was present there. And the entire press conference had for its goal to inform the public on this incident, because we did not want what unfortunately happened subsequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, you heard all the persons who spoke there, including Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I heard Mr. Kordic, and I can say that his speech was very moderate. It was very conciliatory. He did not speak at all badly about the Muslim people, and in general. He simply expressed his outrage against the extremists who had perpetrated a crime and he condemned their act. According to our information, this was done by members of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Their Honours have the transcript of this press conference. We need not belabour this anymore. The transcript speaks for itself. But let me ask you something else. You know that what took place in that press conference was taped and then was rebroadcast on several occasions during that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. This unfortunate incident was covered on several occasions on the local Busovaca television. It was with the aim to inform both the Croatian population and the Muslims, because the local Vitez television could also be seen in Zenica, for instance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And because of the activity that you were involved in, you followed the local media, including Vitez television. Was any other speech, other than the one from the press conference of Mr. Kordic, shown on Vitez television on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I have no other information that any other speech of Mr. Kordic's was broadcast on television on that day, except for what transpired in the press conference which we -- at which we were present that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had anything else been shown you, you would have known about it because of the job that you were in at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. Because of my position, I would have known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the last issue regarding this fighting in Vitez. Together with Zoran Pilicic, you took part in the ceasefire negotiations which took place on the 16th and 17th of April, 1993, under the auspices of UNPROFOR, that is, the BritBat contingent. But on 17 April 1993, another unfortunate incident took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. After the end of the negotiation session, as we were coming back from the BritBat base in Nova Bila, before we entered the headquarters in Hotel Vitez, the British officers did not come right to the hotel, so that they exposed us to the Muslim fire, and I was seriously wounded, and this came from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who wounded you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Members of the Muslim forces from Stari Vitez, because this was open space, and the HVO headquarters was very close to Stari Vitez, where the Muslim forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last question on this, Mr. Prskalo. You recovered in the hospital, and then back home for over three months?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. It took me about three months to recover, because it was a serious wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that I have two or three minutes. I'm moving on to the last area of questioning. Perhaps this would be a good time to break, because I won't be able to finish in two or three minutes. I believe I have no more than 10 minutes left of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now. Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, we have repeatedly mentioned Mr. Dario Kordic. Let us try now to recapitulate what you have already told us and thus bring the examination to a close. You knew Mr. Dario Kordic throughout the war, ever since 1991, because of his political activities, your political activities, and so on and so forth. What was he to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I knew Mr. Kordic throughout the war. To me, he was a politician, basically. He was also a vice-president of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you remember, did he also have some office in the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Likewise, when the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna was proclaimed, he was once again the vice-president of the republic. In other words, he was a politician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand what you said. We first spoke about the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna, but the Croat Republic did not have the office of a vice-president. And you said that he was a vice-president, didn't you, of the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna? The Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna had only a president?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're quite right. My mistake. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your testimony today is basically as to what you knew about the assistant commander for the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia for information and public relations, and that is the angle from which you viewed and interpreted all those things that happened during the war. We've already talked about press conferences, so the press conferences that you, the military, held separately and those which were jointly held by the military and the representatives of the political government of the HVO, primarily Mr. Valenta and people from the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. You viewed them all from the professional angle, that it was your duty to do so, and you must be aware that the Prosecution claims that in late '92 or perhaps -- either at one of the press conferences or perhaps on some other occasion, Mr. Kordic allegedly claimed -- that is, said or delivered a speech in which he threatened to burn the village of Ahmici to the ground unless the roadblock that the ABiH had put up near the Catholic cemetery in Ahmici in October '92 was removed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: That assertion is not correct. I simply cannot understand how somebody could say something, because that is crazy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you heard anybody else publicly utter such a threat, not Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I have never heard anybody say anything like that, regardless of whether it be Croat politicians or military commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today we are addressing, in particular, the press conference held on the 15th of April, '93, in relation to the abduction of the then Colonel Zivko Totic, and we let you go through the videotapes, Z665 and Z665.2. These videotapes are showing that press conference which you attended?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes. I saw those videotapes. These tapes are from that press conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you spoke about the contents of what Mr. Kordic and other participants said on that occasion, so there is no need to go back into that. So let us conclude this, and I've already asked you that. But since we are talking about press conferences, let us round off that topic. On that day, on the 15th, to the best of your knowledge and recollection, Vitez Television aired only that press conference held on the 15th of April, '93, in Busovaca; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say Mr. Kordic was a politician, a political figure, so my question would be: did Mr. Kordic, as a political person, have any powers, any authority, to issue military orders to any HVO unit, including the military police, special-purpose units, or any other?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I can say that Mr. Kordic did not have such powers, such authority; nor did he do that. As far as I know, he did not issue any orders to that effect. It was done by the military, by the HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard any other officer in the HVO mention anything like that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No, I have not, I have never heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, you're aware that Mr. Kordic some addressed as "Sir" and some as "Colonel". You know that he was conferred a rank?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I know that some rank was nominally awarded, but it was a matter of formality and it was to serve some purpose, because he was to attend negotiations at the Sarajevo Airport with representatives of the International Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was when?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: It was sometime in late '92. I cannot remember the date exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout your service with the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, did you ever hear Mr. Kordic use this honourary or formal rank to issue orders or instructions to units or for any military activity?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No. I never heard Mr. Kordic use his rank or issue any orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to conclude, you communicated with a large number of people. You had your officers, who were responsible for information and public relation activities in brigades, and so on and so forth, and you communicated with all HVO members in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, either directly or through your associates. And in that multitude of information that you must have been receiving, have you ever received any information to the effect that Mr. Kordic has ever issued any military order?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Not from any assistant commander for information and public relations in brigades, or from any other officer, have I ever heard that Mr. Kordic had issued any order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, thank you very much for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no further questions. Cross-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, I have two brief questions for you, but I should like to avail myself of your presence here. You mentioned during your testimony that you were in Novi Travnik on the Joint Commission after the October conflict in Novi Travnik in 1992, that is, after the fighting broke out between Croats and Muslims in Novi Travnik. So if I may ask you: You were familiar with the situation in Novi Travnik at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that in Novi Travnik, after that conflict in October 1992, until a broader conflict between Croats and Muslims in April 1993, that the status quo was maintained in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: After that conflict, and after the situation calmed down, after the agreement, and owing to the activities of this commission, I can affirm that there was no more fighting there, apart from individual incidents taking place over a wider area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one question more. You told us a great deal about the early days, about the establishment of the HVO and the situation in Bosnia, the activities on the central government and so on and so forth, at the time when you were an active politician and had better information. Would you agree that a rank-and-file man, an average citizen in Central Bosnia in 1992, could realise that the state did not exist de facto. If you look at what makes a state -- education, health care, police, army -- that it all did not work as it should have, as it should function in a normal state. What could just an ordinary citizen conclude?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: What you said, I could say not only an ordinary man; it was also the perception of other people. It was even my own personal opinion. The state of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not exist anymore. I believe that everybody knows very well that almost every village had a government of its own practically, that every town had something of its own, that to all intents and purposes, not a single institution functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more thing, because I think that the transcript was not quite clear about that. In Vitez, on the 16th of April, when you went to negotiate, you and Mr. Pilicic, you were representing the Operative Zone, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And may I ask you just one more thing, which has never been proved, but I've heard the story, and will you please confirm it for me. Later on, after the war, in 1994, the story was spread around that there was an attempt against you and Pilicic when you were coming back from the negotiations, that this was an organised matter, and that the Bosniak negotiators had let their people in Vitez know by radio that you were coming. Have you heard that story?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that story. And since you raise this, I can tell you that we, the Croats, were not equipped with anything. We did not have any radio or devices. I didn't have any radio device, unlike Muslim representatives. I can even confirm that as we waited for the warriors, the Muslim representative did communicate with his base. And that story, which subsequently began to be spun, leads me to the conclusion that yes, it might be true that they communicated, that it had all been prepared, because the purpose of that shooting was to kill me and Mr. Pilicic, that is, the Croat negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all that I had to ask of this witness Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first ask to think back to all these events, please, Mr. Prskalo, for the purposes of giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: You mean when the lawyers asked me to do that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, the lawyers for Blaskic or lawyers for Kordic. When?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I was -- well, nobody asked me to do that. I offered it. I said I was willing to testify to the truth and the facts, and all my friends and acquaintances knew about that. An acquaintance of mine let me know from Vitez one day that the lawyers would be coming to Split and that I should go there, that I could then present to them my perception, my interpretation of the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that this year or last year?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: It was this year, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By which time, had you followed and heard the results of any of the associated cases in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must now know something of the results of the Blaskic case and the Kupreskic case.

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Sorry, but I just don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you volunteered to go and help, and you are a man with a background in the propaganda department; correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Well, I would not call it propaganda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come to the title of that institution in a minute. When you saw the lawyers, what documents did you have available to you, in your possession, please?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I did not have any documents. All I had was what persisted in my memory, or what I could remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have a diary?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't have at home, where you now live, or anywhere else, and you didn't have access yourself, to any documents dating back to 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to look at any documents when the lawyers spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Well, during that interview, I mean, I did not see any documents. We merely talked about the events of the time and things that I could recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two documents that you've produced today, just help us, please: Where do they come from?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I don't know what documents you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've produced a couple of documents that may not be very important, but they relate to January 1993. Don't you remember producing those two documents?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: What was shown today, what the gentleman from the Defence showed, these are not my documents; they are the documents which the Defence produced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Documents apparently that you signed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes, sure, I did, but I did not bring them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where those documents have been since the time when you signed them and the time when they were produced to you by the Defence lawyers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't have any information as to where HVO documents are kept. I'm sure you'll know that I left the service a long time ago, and even when I was with the service, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But even in the course of meeting lawyers, you were shown no other documents? Either at the time when you met them in Split or at the time when you met them here in The Hague, you were shown no other documents apart from these two; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to the department for which you worked. It was called the Information and Propaganda Department, wasn't it, its formal title?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why were you reluctant to use the word "propaganda" when I said that that was the business in which you were engaged, please?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned that word within the context, if I remember, of a document, and that was not propaganda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I did, but I don't want to take time with that. Is there something about the word "propaganda" that you're unhappy with or that you're uncomfortable with the word "propaganda"?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A man called Bozo Rajic, in October of 1992, set out terms of reference on which you would be working, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Well, a programme had been put on paper for the work of the information and propaganda department. That is true. But I don't know if the Court knows that Mr. Rajic was the first IPD, information and propaganda man there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you accept that the three criterion that he set out for IPD personnel like yourself were, one, that they must be proven fighters for the idea of the HZ HB [realtime transcript read in error "HDZ"]; two, that they must be communicative and gifted when dealing with people; and, three, that they must fit into their working environment or the environment where they are supposed to work? Would you accept that those were the three criteria he set out for people working in the propaganda department?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I have to say that I do not remember all that it said there, all that was written there. But from what I do remember, there were no political criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. We heard, in Croatian, that HZ HB was said, and the transcript says "HDZ", so I don't know who made the slip. The Prosecutor mentioned HDZ, the ideas of the HDZ, or the HZ HB? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I should have mentioned and I hope I mentioned "HZ HB".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prskalo, would you accept that you qualify as a proven fighter for the idea of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: I cannot answer in this way, because I was part of the army, that is, the HVO, with a view to performing the tasks set before the IPD.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you accept that the IPD was itself divided into three branches; first, the information and propaganda administration; second, the administration for military and preventative psychology; and, third, the administration for history, publishing, culture, sports, and recreation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure if it was organised in that way. Some of it may have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And certainly if it was organised in that way, your role was fairly and squarely in the information and propaganda administration sector of the department?

utterances.speaker: MARKO PRSKALO
